newsitem.title: UK: UK labour turnover 16 percent in 1996 - CBI.
newsitem.headline: UK labour turnover 16 percent in 1996 - CBI.

text.p: Sixteen out of every 100 UK employees left their jobs last year, mostly of their own volition, according to a new survey from the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) published on Monday.
The CBI plans to publish the survey on an annual basis to give firms a benchmark against which to measure their staff turnover.

"Labour turnover is to some degree inevitable and can be a positive force for employers, as it can create the opportunity to introduce people with new ideas and new experiences into the workplace," said John Cridland, CBI director of human resources policy.

"But high levels of turnover can be a problem, and in particular can be expensive -- as well as the direct costs of recruiting and subsequent training of replacement, there are the indirect costs in terms of lost production, reduced performance and even lower morale," he said.
There was considerable variation between different sectors with some areas having very high turnover of staff -- such as retail and wholesale, at 39.2 percent, and hotel and leisure at 23.7 percent.
Other areas saw much lower turnover of staff, with local government at just 6.5 percent and manufacturing at 6.7 percent.
There was a different pattern for full and part time employees. One in four part-time employees -- 25.2 percent -- left their jobs in 1996 compared with one in ten -- 11.6 percent -- of full timers.

The majority of leavers, some 70 percent of full time workers and 90 percent of part-time, stated that they were leaving voluntarily while 22 percent of full time employees were made redundant compared with only four percent of part-time leavers.
The CBI said 616 organisations took part in the survey, representing a combined workforce of just under 1.5 million employees.
